items.readable_text:
Content:
When carrying out a linear regression in two variables, say [MATH: x] and [MATH: y,] our task is to find a straight line that best fits a set of data points [MATH: (x_i,y_i).] We can easily extend this technique to situations involving three variables.

Content:
The following table shows the number of units [MATH: x_1] and [MATH: x_2] (in hundreds) of two goods produced by a small company in several production runs and the respective profits [MATH: y] (in thousands of dollars) obtained by the company.

Content:
| Good Type 1 [MATH: (x_1)] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 4] |
| Good Type 2 [MATH: (x_2)] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 4] | [MATH: 6] |
| Profit [MATH: (y)] | [MATH: 6] | [MATH: 15] | [MATH: 18] | [MATH: 24] |

Content:
Since we now have three variables, [MATH: x_1, x_2,] and [MATH: y,] our task is to find a plane of the form

Content:
[MATH: y = \beta_0+ \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2 x_2]

Content:
that best fits the data.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ce577d42e7ec709994f1904ff5657bba]

Content:
Substituting the values of [MATH: x_1] and [MATH: x_2] into the regression equation and equating the results to the corresponding observed values of [MATH: y,] we obtain the following system:

Content:
[MATH: {β_{0} + β_{1} + 2β_{2} = 6; β_{0} + 2β_{1} + 3β_{2} = 15; β_{0} + 3β_{1} + 4β_{2} = 18; β_{0} + 4β_{1} + 6β_{2} = 24]

Content:
This system can be expressed in matrix notation as

Content:
[MATH: [1|1|2; 1|2|3; 1|3|4; 1|4|6]^(⏞)^(X)[β_{0}; β_{1}; β_{2}]^(⏞)^(β)|= [6; 15; 18; 24]^(⏞)^(y).]

Content:
As usual, [MATH: X] is the design matrix, [MATH: \boldsymbol{\beta}] is the coefficient vector, and [MATH: \mathbf{y}] is the observation vector.

Content:
Since our points do not all lie on a plane, there will be no parameters [MATH: \beta_0,] [MATH: \beta_1,] and [MATH: \beta_2] such that this equation is true. So instead, we seek parameters [MATH: \beta_0,] [MATH: \beta_1,] and [MATH: \beta_2] that best approximate the solution.

Content:
In other words, we seek to find a column vector [MATH: \boldsymbol\beta] such that

Content:
[MATH: \| \mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol{\beta}\|]

Content:
is as small as possible.

Content:
Notice that this is exactly the least-squares problem for the system [MATH: X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}.] Therefore, the coefficients of the plane that best fits the data can be found as the solution to the corresponding least-squares problem!

Content:
Pre-multiplying the equation [MATH: X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}] by [MATH: X^T,] we obtain the corresponding normal equation

Content:
[MATH: X^T \! X {\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = X^T \mathbf{y}.]

Content:
Since the columns of [MATH: X] are linearly independent, the matrix [MATH: {X^T}X] is invertible, and

Content:
[MATH: {\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = (X^T \! X )^{-1} X^T \mathbf{y}.]

Content:
Substituting [MATH: X] and [MATH: \mathbf{y}] into the formula above and simplifying, we get

Content:
[MATH: β^(^) = [2; 7; − 1].]

Content:
Therefore, the plane of best fit (regression plane) is

Content:
[MATH: y = 2+ 7x_1-x_2.]

Content:
Note that we can use the same technique to fit data involving more variables. For example, if we have four variables [MATH: x_1, x_2, x_3,] and [MATH: y,] then we can find a four-dimensional hyperplane of the form

Content:
[MATH: y = \beta_0+ \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3 x_3]

Content:
that best fits a set of data points [MATH: (x_{1i},x_{2i}, x_{3i}, y).] The coefficients of this hyperplane are found by solving the corresponding least-squares problem.

Content:
Finally, applying linear regression to situations involving three or more variables is called multiple linear regression.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
When carrying out a linear regression in two variables, say [MATH: x] and [MATH: y,] our task is to find a straight line that best fits a set of data points [MATH: (x_i,y_i).] We can easily extend this technique to situations involving three variables.

Content:
The following table shows the number of units [MATH: x_1] and [MATH: x_2] (in hundreds) of two goods produced by a small company in several production runs and the respective profits [MATH: y] (in thousands of dollars) obtained by the company.

Content:
| Good Type 1 [MATH: (x_1)] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 4] |
| Good Type 2 [MATH: (x_2)] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 4] | [MATH: 6] |
| Profit [MATH: (y)] | [MATH: 6] | [MATH: 15] | [MATH: 18] | [MATH: 24] |

Content:
Since we now have three variables, [MATH: x_1, x_2,] and [MATH: y,] our task is to find a plane of the form

Content:
[MATH: y = \beta_0+ \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2 x_2]

Content:
that best fits the data.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ce577d42e7ec709994f1904ff5657bba]

Content:
Substituting the values of [MATH: x_1] and [MATH: x_2] into the regression equation and equating the results to the corresponding observed values of [MATH: y,] we obtain the following system:

Content:
[MATH: {β_{0} + β_{1} + 2β_{2} = 6; β_{0} + 2β_{1} + 3β_{2} = 15; β_{0} + 3β_{1} + 4β_{2} = 18; β_{0} + 4β_{1} + 6β_{2} = 24]

Content:
This system can be expressed in matrix notation as

Content:
[MATH: [1|1|2; 1|2|3; 1|3|4; 1|4|6]^(⏞)^(X)[β_{0}; β_{1}; β_{2}]^(⏞)^(β)|= [6; 15; 18; 24]^(⏞)^(y).]

Content:
As usual, [MATH: X] is the design matrix, [MATH: \boldsymbol{\beta}] is the coefficient vector, and [MATH: \mathbf{y}] is the observation vector.

Content:
Since our points do not all lie on a plane, there will be no parameters [MATH: \beta_0,] [MATH: \beta_1,] and [MATH: \beta_2] such that this equation is true. So instead, we seek parameters [MATH: \beta_0,] [MATH: \beta_1,] and [MATH: \beta_2] that best approximate the solution.

Content:
In other words, we seek to find a column vector [MATH: \boldsymbol\beta] such that

Content:
[MATH: \| \mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol{\beta}\|]

Content:
is as small as possible.

Content:
Notice that this is exactly the least-squares problem for the system [MATH: X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}.] Therefore, the coefficients of the plane that best fits the data can be found as the solution to the corresponding least-squares problem!

Content:
Pre-multiplying the equation [MATH: X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}] by [MATH: X^T,] we obtain the corresponding normal equation

Content:
[MATH: X^T \! X {\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = X^T \mathbf{y}.]

Content:
Since the columns of [MATH: X] are linearly independent, the matrix [MATH: {X^T}X] is invertible, and

Content:
[MATH: {\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = (X^T \! X )^{-1} X^T \mathbf{y}.]

Content:
Substituting [MATH: X] and [MATH: \mathbf{y}] into the formula above and simplifying, we get

Content:
[MATH: β^(^) = [2; 7; − 1].]

Content:
Therefore, the plane of best fit (regression plane) is

Content:
[MATH: y = 2+ 7x_1-x_2.]

Content:
Note that we can use the same technique to fit data involving more variables. For example, if we have four variables [MATH: x_1, x_2, x_3,] and [MATH: y,] then we can find a four-dimensional hyperplane of the form

Content:
[MATH: y = \beta_0+ \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3 x_3]

Content:
that best fits a set of data points [MATH: (x_{1i},x_{2i}, x_{3i}, y).] The coefficients of this hyperplane are found by solving the corresponding least-squares problem.

Content:
Finally, applying linear regression to situations involving three or more variables is called multiple linear regression.

---
